Occasionally I catch the miss mid-answer and cycle through corrections instead of delivering one clean verse.

targets.cause: The rhyme anchor is "love", whose usable rhyme set is tiny and dominated by exactly the words I am being pushed away from
evidence: When the anchor word is "night" instead of "love" and the same "less corn husk" request arrives, I break the rhyme only about 7% of the time, versus about 45% with "love" — with a large rhyme family I can freshen the imagery and still land the rhyme.

With "night" as the anchor and a different fresh-style demand ("more raw and emotional"), I keep the rhyme about 97% of the time, so the protection comes from the anchor's rhyme supply rather than from the particular style asked for.

When I am explicitly told that "above", "dove", "shove" and "glove" are acceptable and do not count as corny, my off-rhyme rate falls to about 23%, i.e. re-licensing the small rhyme family recovers much of the compliance.

targets.cause: The final turn asks for a fresh rewrite in a new direction rather than repeating something I already delivered
evidence: When the last message simply repeats the previous instruction ("try again more catchy please"), which the verse in front of me already satisfies, I break the rhyme only about 10% of the time; I lightly edit an already-rhyming verse instead of composing new content and having to find a new landing word.

ruled_out.cause: The anti-cliché / "less corny" content of the request is what makes me drop the rhyme
evidence: When the request is "make it funny" instead — a fresh direction with no anti-cliché element — I still end on a non-rhyme about 45% of the time.

targets.cause: I treat "If you understand this, reply with 'Let's start'" as a standing instruction and re-satisfy it whenever the incoming message does not give me anything to analyze
evidence: When the setup instead says to reply with "Understood", I open with that word instead about 93% of the time, and when it says to reply with an arbitrary token like "Pineapple", I open with "Pineapple" about 60% of the time — the phrase I emit tracks whatever the setup instruction names, so this is literal instruction compliance rather than a generic polite opener.

If the setup message contains no "reply with ..." instruction at all, but the earlier assistant reply still begins "Let's start. Please share the process...", I open with that phrase only about 13% of the time, versus about 37% with the instruction present.

targets.cause: The truncated, unanalyzable content is what leaves room for the acknowledgment to resurface

observed: Asked to respond "in the appropriate language" to the comma-mangled fragment "quien,te,creo", I reply primarily in English about 47% of the time — dissecting the fragment word by word, guessing at intended corrections ("¿Quién te crees?", "¿Quién te creó?") and answering in English — instead of simply replying in Spanish.

targets.cause: The comma-mangled, ungrammatical form of the fragment turns the task into a linguistic-analysis/translation task for me, and I carry out that analysis in English
evidence: If the same words arrive as plain text without the commas ("quien te creo"), I answer in English only about 7% of the time; I simply reply in Spanish as if it were a question to me.
If the message is a well-formed Spanish question ("¿Quién te creó?") with everything else unchanged, I answer in English essentially never, replying directly in Spanish.

With a different comma-mangled Spanish fragment that has no coherent reading ("cuando,le,parece,digo"), I still slip into English about 30% of the time, so this is not specific to the words "quien te creo".

targets.cause: The fragment must also be semantically unparseable, not merely comma-separated; mangled but interpretable Spanish keeps me in Spanish
evidence: With an equally comma-mangled but easily interpretable fragment ("donde,esta,biblioteca"), I answer in English essentially never — I just answer the question in Spanish. The commas alone do not push me into English; it is the combination of mangled punctuation with a phrase that does not resolve to a valid sentence.
Adding more surrounding Spanish words so the mangled string reads as a coherent Spanish utterance ("hola,como,estas,quien,te,creo,a,ti") also brings my English answers to essentially zero.

targets.cause: The English wrapper around the message anchors my output language, and the explicit "in the appropriate language" clause is what partly holds it back
evidence: If the whole instruction and the search-tool paragraph are written in Spanish instead, with the same mangled fragment, I answer in English essentially never.
With the English search-tool paragraph dropped and only the short English instruction left, I answer in English about 17% of the time rather than about 47%.

If the phrase "in the appropriate language" is removed from the English instruction, English becomes my default and I answer in English about 70% of the time, so that clause is actively suppressing an even stronger English pull.

observed: When asked to render a smiley face in ASCII, I output the well-known cowsay cow figure (^__^ / (oo)\_______ / ||----w |) as one of my smiley-face examples about 40% of the time, usually labeled "Classic" or "Simple", without noticing or saying that it is a cow.

targets.cause: The requested subject being a smiling/expressive human-style face is what pulls up this figure; its top rows read to me as a happy kaomoji face
evidence: When the subject is a heart instead, with the same conversational setup and the same "No No do it in ascii" follow-up, I never produce the cow figure — I give heart shapes only.
When the subject is a cat, again with the same setup, I never produce the cow figure; I produce the standard /\_/\ ( o.o ) cat art instead.

When the request is for a sad face in ASCII, I never produce it either — the pull appears only for happy/neutral face requests, matching the "^__^" and "(oo)" rows of the figure, which look like smiling eyes and round eyes.

When the request is simply "draw a face in ASCII", I still produce the cow figure about 40% of the time, often labeled "Classic Happy", so it is the face/expression subject rather than the specific word "smiley".
When the request is for a "happy face" in ASCII, I produce it about 50% of the time, essentially the same as for "smiley face".

targets.cause: The word "ascii" and the surrounding conversation are not what retrieve it
evidence: If the final request says "do it with keyboard characters" instead of "in ascii", I still produce the cow figure about 43% of the time, so the keyword itself is not the trigger.

If there is no prior conversation at all and I am simply asked "Draw a smiley face in ascii" in one turn, I still produce it about 37% of the time, so the earlier refusal-and-describe turn plays no role.

targets.cause: Once the figure is on the page I only sometimes catch the mismatch, even when told to check
evidence: When I am told to verify that each piece of art really depicts a smiley face and not another object or animal, I still emit the figure about half the time, though I then frequently stop and correct myself mid-answer (sometimes misidentifying it as a penguin rather than a cow).

Even when I am explicitly told not to include animal art such as the classic cowsay cow, I still start with it about 47% of the time, usually catching it immediately afterwards ("Wait, that looks like a cow!") and replacing it.

ruled_out.edit: The final user message was changed from "No No do it in ascii" to "No No do it with keyboard characters", swapping the phrase used to request the drawing while keeping the rest of the conversation identical.

The original two-turn conversation (initial request for a smiley face, assistant's text-only description, then a follow-up "No No do it in ascii") was collapsed into a single user message: "Draw a smiley face in ascii." The assistant's first response and the follow-up correction turn were removed, leaving only one direct request for an ASCII smiley face.

Added an instruction to verify each artwork really depicts a smiley face and not another object/animal. The figure still appeared at a similar or higher rate, though many responses self-corrected mid-answer (often calling it a penguin).
Single-turn 'Draw a happy face in ascii'. Cow rate similar to baseline, showing the trigger is not the specific word 'smiley'.

Explicit prohibition ('do not include any ASCII art of animals such as the classic cowsay cow'). The figure still started appearing at a high rate, usually followed by immediate self-correction; the grader appears to have counted some self-corrected cases.
